title: Evening prayer
hook: Jacob's prayer, said as night falls

segments.voice: Yesterday, aneni, Elijah's cry answered at the afternoon offering. Your line was heard in the afternoon. Today, the sun goes down.

A young man is running away from home. He's fooled his father, and his brother wants him dead. He walks until the sun sets on the road to Haran: nowhere to sleep, no inn, no tent. He puts a stone under his head and lies down in the open. That night he'll dream of a ladder with angels on it. But before the dream, there's a small verb in the text that the rabbis noticed. And from that verb, they found the evening prayer.
screen: `RUNNING AWAY FROM HOME.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `BEFORE THE DREAM.`

segments.voice: Genesis, in the old Jewish translation: "And he lighted upon the place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set." Lighted upon, in Hebrew vayifga: he came upon, he met, he ran into. The Talmud, in Berakhot, says that same verb can mean to plead or to pray, and reads it here as prayer. So Abraham has the morning, Isaac the afternoon, and Jacob, alone on the road at sundown, the night. The evening prayer is called Maariv, from its first blessing, which praises God who brings on the evenings, ma'ariv aravim. Some communities call it Arvit, from the same root, evening. Now a surprising piece of history. The Talmud records an argument about whether the evening prayer was required at all. One sage said it was optional; another, an obligation. There's a famous, tense story of the academy's leaders clashing over it. In time, it became a fixed part of every day, but a trace of the argument is still there. At Maariv, the leader doesn't repeat the Amidah aloud, the way they do in the morning and afternoon. Everyone says it silently, and the service moves on. One more detail. The Talmud ties the morning and afternoon prayers to the Temple's two daily offerings. For the night, it can only point to what was left burning on the altar until morning. There was no evening offering of its own. Just, in the story, a person on a road, meeting the place where he stopped.
screen: `HE LIGHTED UPON THE PLACE.` · `JACOB GETS THE NIGHT.` · `ONCE ARGUED AS OPTIONAL.` · `NO REPETITION ALOUD.` · then, large: `EVENING PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Wherever you'll be when the light goes, that's your place, the way the roadside was Jacob's; look outside if it's dark, or picture this evening's sunset, and slowly notice the room, the street, the sky. If you pray, offer an evening prayer in any words you have; if not, just meet the place you've landed.
Maariv. The one who brings on evening. The night prayer, traced to Jacob meeting the place at sunset.
Your line: meet the place you've landed. Even a roadside can be the place. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Maariv is said after nightfall: Barchu, the Shema with its blessings, and the Amidah said silently without a repetition aloud, followed by Aleinu; many people say it right after Mincha, near sunset.

chat.says: Where does the Jewish evening prayer come from? Who started it?
options: The Talmud traces it to Jacob, who met the place on the road at sunset.
It was added in modern times, for people who work all day long.
It was written in the Middle Ages, as a prayer for travelers far from home.
chat.meaning: The Talmud reads vayifga, he lighted upon the place, as prayer: Jacob, alone at sundown, gets the night.

notes: Genesis 28:11 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Berakhot 26b: pegi'ah means prayer (citing Jeremiah 7:16); paraphrased.
Berakhot 27b–28a: Rabban Gamliel vs Rabbi Joshua on whether Arvit is optional, and the deposition story; referred to as 'a famous, tense story'.
The halachic link between the 'optional' status and the absence of a repetition is the standard explanation; confirm.

Editor review (y2 595–612): the teach said 'the night has no offering' and that the evening prayer is said 'after dark has begun'; Berakhot 26b links Arvit to the limbs and fats burned on the altar overnight, and many say Maariv before dark right after Mincha (as howItsDone says). Both lines rewritten. 'In the end, Jews took it on' softened to 'in time, it became'.
